title: The tabernacle and the red lamp
hookLine: the lamp burning beside it tells you the Eucharist is reserved there

lines: A SMALL FLAME IN RED GLASS.
A LIGHT ON IN THE WINDOW.
cards: A Catholic church on a weekday afternoon. It's quiet. Maybe an older man in the back pew, maybe nobody at all.
The lights are low. Near the front, usually to one side, a small flame burns steadily in a red glass. It burns all night when the doors are locked.
It burns on holidays. Drive past a house at three in the morning, see a light on in the window, and you'd think: someone's home. Catholics mean something like that.

teach.h: A LOCKED BOX, A LAMP BESIDE IT.
teach.b: The flame is the sanctuary lamp, and it burns beside the tabernacle: a small, locked box, often gold, sometimes a little house of carved wood or stone. Inside are consecrated hosts left over from Mass.

Catholics believe Jesus is truly present in them, so the tabernacle is kept with great honor. Church law says a special lamp should burn before it at all times, to show and honor that presence; red is the usual custom.

teach.h: IF IT'S LIT, THE HOST IS KEPT HERE.
teach.b: So the lamp is a sign you can read from the door: if it's lit, the Eucharist is reserved here. That's why Catholics genuflect, bending the right knee to the floor, when they pass the tabernacle. Why keep hosts at all?

First, for the sick and dying: the Catechism says the Eucharist was first reserved so it could be carried to those who couldn't come to Mass. Over time, people also began to come and pray before it. Now the word.
Tabernacle comes from the Latin tabernaculum, a tent. In the book of Exodus, while Israel wandered in the desert, God asked for a tent to be made so he could live among the people.
In the Douay-Rheims: "And they shall make me a sanctuary, and I will dwell in the midst of them." That tent was the tabernacle, and a lamp burned in it too.
John's Gospel picks up the image: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."
In Greek, dwelt literally means pitched his tent.

teach.h: I WILL DWELL IN THE MIDST OF THEM.
teach.b: So the little box in the church carries a long story: God wanting to live next door, in a tent, among his people.

how: Catholics genuflect toward the tabernacle when they enter or pass it, and many stop in a church during the day to pray quietly near the sanctuary lamp.

o: the small room where confessions are heard
the tall reading stand where Scripture is proclaimed
the locked box in church where the Eucharist is kept

games.q: you walk into a dim, empty church and see a small red flame near the front. what does it tell you?
o: someone forgot to blow out a candle.
the Eucharist is reserved in the tabernacle here.
a funeral is about to start.
games.why: the sanctuary lamp burns beside the tabernacle to show and honor the Eucharist kept there.

practice: Picture a church you know, try to remember where its red lamp is, and imagine sitting quietly near the flame. You don't have to say anything.
If you pray, simply say hello, the way you would to someone home; if you don't, notice what it's like to sit near a light that never goes out.

wordCard.voice: Tabernacle. From the Latin for a tent. The place in a church where the Eucharist is kept, with a lamp burning beside it. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, John 1:14: he dwelt, literally he pitched his tent, from skene, a tent.

carryVoice: Your line: someone is home. For Catholics, a small red flame says so, day and night. Rest well.
